lessons.title: Elements of literary texts
lessons.html:
Why study literature at work?

Evaluating literary texts develops the ability to read closely, interpret meaning, recognise how language persuades and moves people, and form and defend judgements. These skills transfer directly to business: reading between the lines of a supplier letter, understanding a customer's point of view, and communicating persuasively. Literature also deepens understanding of the South African rural experience, from land and labour to drought, community and change.

Genres

  • Prose fiction: novels and short stories.
  • Poetry: including praise poetry (izibongo) and contemporary verse.
  • Drama: plays written for performance.
  • Oral literature: folktales, proverbs and songs passed down by speech.

Elements to analyse in prose and drama

ElementQuestions to ask
PlotWhat happens? What is the conflict? How is it resolved?
CharacterWho are the main characters? How are they revealed: through actions, speech, others' views? Do they change?
SettingWhere and when? A farm, a township, a drought-stricken valley? How does setting shape events?
Point of viewWho tells the story? First person, third person? How reliable is the narrator?
ThemeWhat larger ideas does the text explore: land, belonging, justice, family, survival?
Style and toneWord choice, imagery, sentence rhythm, humour, irony

Elements in poetry

Consider imagery (pictures created with words), figurative language (metaphor, simile, personification), sound (rhyme, rhythm, alliteration, repetition), structure (stanzas, line breaks) and tone. Read a poem aloud; sound is part of its meaning.

lessons.title: Methods of evaluation
lessons.html:
From understanding to evaluation

Evaluation goes beyond summary. It asks how well a text achieves its effects, how it reflects or challenges its context, and what its value is for readers.

A reading process

  1. First reading: read for overall understanding and personal response. What did you feel and why?
  2. Close reading: reread key passages. Annotate images, repeated words, shifts in tone, important dialogue.
  3. Analysis: connect techniques to meaning. How does the writer's choice of a single, cracked borehole as an image make drought feel personal?
  4. Context: consider when and where the text was written, and the writer's background. A novel written during apartheid about farm labour carries a different weight than one written today.
  5. Evaluation: judge effectiveness, relevance and value, with evidence.

Criteria for evaluation

  • Craft: is the language precise and vivid? Is the structure purposeful?
  • Characterisation: are characters believable and complex?
  • Insight: does the text offer fresh understanding of people, society or experience?
  • Impact: does it move, provoke or challenge the reader?
  • Representation: whose voices are heard or silenced? Are groups portrayed fairly or stereotypically?

Example

Alan Paton's novel Cry, the Beloved Country (1948) opens with a description of the hills of Natal and the eroded valleys below. A reader might evaluate how this landscape description links the damaged land to the damaged society, and also consider critics' views about how the novel represents its black characters. Evaluation weighs strengths and limitations.

Comparing texts

Comparing two texts on a similar theme, for example two poems about land, sharpens judgement: how does each handle the theme, and which is more effective for its purpose and audience?

lessons.title: Expressing an evaluation
lessons.html:
Writing or speaking your evaluation

An evaluation must be clear, structured and supported.

Structure

  1. Introduction: name the text, author, genre and your overall judgement (thesis).
  2. Body paragraphs: each makes one point, supported by evidence (a quotation or specific reference) and explanation of how the evidence supports the point.
  3. Counter-view: acknowledge a different reading and respond to it.
  4. Conclusion: restate your judgement and its significance.

Using evidence

Use short, accurate quotations and explain them. A useful pattern is Point, Evidence, Explanation (PEE). Do not simply retell the plot; the reader of your evaluation wants your analysis, not a summary.

Language of evaluation

  • "The writer effectively conveys..."
  • "This image is powerful because..."
  • "However, the characterisation of ... is less convincing, as..."
  • "Compared with ..., this poem..."

Respecting other views

Literature invites different interpretations. A strong evaluation is open to other readings while defending its own with evidence. In group discussion, listen, ask questions and respond to the argument, not the person.

Transferring the skill

The same process applies to evaluating a supplier's brochure, a competitor's advertisement or a customer's letter: identify the purpose and techniques, test claims against evidence, and reach a supported judgement.

Key points

  • Analyse plot, character, setting, point of view, theme, style and tone.
  • In poetry, consider imagery, figurative language, sound and structure.
  • Evaluation judges craft, insight, impact and representation, in context.
  • Support every judgement with evidence and explanation.
  • Acknowledge other interpretations and respond to them.
